title: A Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM): Proportionate Access and Capability Limits for Comprehensive Frontier AI Safety
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 14 Oct 2026]
Title:A Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM): Proportionate Access and Capability Limits for Comprehensive Frontier AI Safety
View PDF
            Abstract:Most debate about releasing capable AI systems treats the choice as binary: keep the model behind an API, or publish the weights. That framing runs together two separate decisions. One is how capable a system may become. The other is who may obtain a given capability, and on what terms. This paper is about the second decision. We propose a Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM) that sorts access by purpose, safety, and capability instead of by release artifact. Tier 1, AI for Learning, is broadly accessible and deliberately capability-bounded. Tier 2, AI for Exploration, serves research and development under registration, identity, and usage controls that tighten as capability rises. Tier 3, Full-Scale Frontier AI, is available only through structured, recorded, and accountable access. The principle behind the tiers is that accessibility should be proportional to capability, safety, and risk. We show why publishing frontier-class weights forfeits every safety lever a developer has after release, and, using evidence that safety fine-tuning can be stripped from open weights for a few hundred dollars, why an evaluation of the base model says little about its derivatives. We give criteria for assigning a system to a tier along capability, autonomy, domain-consequence, and usage/safety axes, and combine MAIAM with the SAFE AI Operating Point into a two-part framework: a Capability Boundary that fixes the safety limits not to be crossed, and an Accessibility Boundary that fixes who may obtain a capability below that limit. Capability limits alone do not make AI safe; a tiered access regime administered by regulating bodies is also needed.

report.summary: Paper proposes MAIAM, a tiered access model that governs who gets frontier AI capabilities by purpose, safety, and risk, rather than binary API-or-weights release.
report.background: Debate over releasing capable AI systems is often framed as a binary choice: keep the model behind an API or publish the weights. This conflates two decisions: how capable a system may become, and who may obtain that capability and under what terms. The paper focuses on the second decision. As open-weight models proliferate, evidence shows safety fine-tuning can be stripped cheaply, meaning base-model evaluations reveal little about derivative risks. MAIAM responds by sorting access by purpose, safety, and capability. It combines with the SAFE AI Operating Point to separate a Capability Boundary from an Accessibility Boundary, arguing that capability limits alone cannot make AI safe without a tiered access regime administered by regulators.
key_points: MAIAM separates capability limits from access controls. Tier 1, AI for Learning, is broadly accessible but deliberately capability-bounded. Tier 2, AI for Exploration, serves research and development under registration, identity, and usage controls that tighten as capability rises. Tier 3, Full-Scale Frontier AI, is available only through structured, recorded, and accountable access. Access is proportional to capability, safety, and risk.

Publishing frontier-class weights forfeits every post-release safety lever. Once weights are public, developers cannot revoke access, monitor misuse, or patch dangerous derivatives. The paper cites evidence that safety fine-tuning can be removed from open weights for a few hundred dollars, showing that evaluating a base model says little about what its derivatives can do.

The framework gives criteria for assigning systems to tiers along four axes: capability, autonomy, domain-consequence, and usage/safety. This moves classification away from release artifacts like API versus weights and toward intended purpose, deployment context, and risk. Regulators could use these axes to set proportionate controls.

MAIAM combines with the SAFE AI Operating Point into a two-part framework. A Capability Boundary fixes safety limits not to be crossed. An Accessibility Boundary fixes who may obtain a capability below that limit. The authors argue capability limits alone do not make AI safe; a tiered access regime administered by regulating bodies is also needed.
report.impact: For the AI industry, MAIAM pushes firms away from binary open-versus-closed release strategies toward graduated access, licensing, identity checks, and auditable use. Large labs may face compliance burdens and regulatory oversight, while open-source communities could see registration or capability thresholds. Developers would need tier-aware APIs, logging, and evaluation pipelines, especially for frontier systems. Regular users might gain safer deployments but lose unrestricted access to the most capable models, with possible gatekeeping and slower diffusion. The framework could shape future AI regulation, procurement, and international coordination, though enforcement across borders and open-weight leakage remain difficult.
report.tools: No code or dataset accompanies this policy paper. Readers can follow up via arXiv, alphaXiv for discussion, Connected Papers and Litmaps for citation mapping, and Hugging Face for open-weight model cards. For capability and safety evaluation, watch METR, HELM, OpenAI Evals, and the SAFE AI Operating Point framework. These help track how tiered access proposals intersect with practical model evaluation and governance.
